utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I have a very -- I think a very short matter to mention, Your Honours. The Trial Chamber, Your Honours, directed that the Petkovic Defence should serve any motion that it proposed to put in for the admission of documents other than through witnesses by a date which is now the 31st of March. Your Honours, at the same time the Trial Chamber will be aware that -- I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic has corrected me. The 21st. I'm sorry, I slipped. The 21st, not the 31st. At the same time, Your Honours will be aware that there are pending applications for admission of documents through witnesses. Your Honour, a position arises which also arose in relation to at least one of the other Defences, where, of course, it is possible that Your Honours would refuse admission of a document on the application for it to be admitted through a witness, but, nevertheless, there may be scope for us to ask for it to be admitted under a different guide-line other than through a witness. We simply wanted to clear with Your Honours, with respect, that the procedure which was previously adopted, particularly in relation to the Stojic Defence, is acceptable, that although we are about to file the motion that Your Honours directed we should file, filed by the 21st of March, that we may nevertheless serve a further or supplementary motion if, following refusal of admission of documents through witnesses, we feel that there is a proper application to be made for them to be admitted under the other guide-line, not through a witness. I just wanted to be sure. We didn't want Your Honours then to say, Well, you're too late, we directed that you should deal with this in that motion. It's just that, really, out of caution, and we do suggest, Your Honour, this is a sensible and practical procedural course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask my colleagues what they feel about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, the Chamber has deliberated and feels that you should proceed as did the Coric Defence; namely, that it is in the interest of everyone, and especially of your team, to file this motion after having learned, if it happens that some evidence was rejected once witnesses have testified, if any document or exhibit is rejected, then you can include those documents that may have been rejected in this new motion. Have you understood what I was trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think I have, subject to just being absolutely sure that Your Honours -- Your Honours are agreeing with us that we should file our main motion for admission of documents other than through witnesses, as planned, on the 21st, and then there would be a supplemental motion. That is what I was asking, and I understand Your Honours to be agreeing with that. And I see lots of nodding of heads, which I'm always very happy to see, of course. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Very well. I seize this opportunity to greet everyone. I would like to greet the witness. I would like to greet the accused, as well as the various counsels in the courtroom. I would also like to greet Mr. Bos, Mr. Scott, as well as everybody else from the OTP. Mr. Bos, you have 54 minutes and 30 seconds to wrap up. I will give you a credit of an additional 30 seconds. In other words, you have 54 minutes or perhaps 55 minutes. And then we will move to redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I hope I won't need those extra 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. I want to talk to you today -- I want to start with an incident that occurred around late July 1993, when you were sent to Prozor with a unit from the 2nd Light Assault Battalion for a combat operation which was led by General Praljak. I don't know if you remember, but in order to refresh your memory I'll ask you to look at the document, a report that you've written about this, which is P03792. Now, sir, this is a handwritten report from you, dated the 29th of July. The English translation reads "the 20th of July," but I think if you look at the original, it should read "the 29th of July." And let me just ask you: Is that your handwriting? Is this your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, in order to get familiarised with what happened and what you reported, I think I'll read out the first five paragraphs of this report so that everyone knows what went on. And I'll read it out slowly: "On 27 July 1993, in obedience to an order received, a unit of the 2nd Luka Jozic Light Assault Battalion from Livno was sent to report to the Prozor operational zone, where they were supposed to receive detailed orders on their tasks. On arrival at Prozor, General Praljak had already planned an attack on and capture of Voljic village in Uskoplje municipality. Since we were not familiar with the field, we received an order from General Praljak to reconnoiter and prepare the field for an attack on and capture of Duratbegov Dolac village. The same assignment was received by a unit of the Professional Battalion of the Petar Kresimir IV Brigade from Livno. "Upon receiving the order, we went to the Duratbegov Dolac sector, where we reconnoitered the field, gathered intelligence about the enemy, and we returned to the Prozor OZ, where we reported on the situation. "A conversation with General Praljak led to an argument between the commander of the Professional Battalion and the general. "The quarrel, in the main, related to the execution of combat assignments, because the commander of the professional battalion asked for more personnel and equipment to carry out the assignment. I, too, was convinced of the need for this. "General Praljak then said that he would dismiss me and my unit and that I would command no longer. The commander of the Professional Battalion said that I had received an order to reconnoiter the field from Mr. Coric, to which the general replied that he had told Coric a hundred times that he gave the orders, and he was now telling me for the first and last time, and that next time I would be locked up, along with the unit. Mr. Filipovic also took part in this conversation, and he addressed the following words to the commander of the Professional Battalion, and I quote: 'I've had it up here with you pricks from Livno,' after which the commander of the Professional Battalion and his unit left the Prozor municipality." Now, sir, do you recall what's been reported here, and do you have anything to add as to what I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we had received a task to report to Prozor, the 2nd Assault Battalion of the Military Police. I was also in Prozor when those incidents happened, and I know that the 2nd Light Assault Battalion and the Professional Battalion from the Livno Brigade received an order from General Praljak to scout the terrain and to engage in combat immediately. The commanders then said that they needed some more time to prepare the terrain, to prepare their men, and to co-ordinate with the other units on both the left and the right flanks. The situation was tense. I am not denying that. There was an argument. The only thing that is not true in this report is the fact that the commander of the Professional Battalion from the Livno Brigade interfered, and he spoke on behalf of the military police, and he mentioned Valentin Coric, who was not his superior at all. And this paragraph that I wrote, it means that the commander of the Professional Battalion mentioned and evoked the name of Mr. Coric, and he was not supposed to, because he was not his commander. The conflict in question was between the Livno Brigade and General Praljak, and it involved a failure to carry out some order. General Praljak, the way he is a bit fast in his reactions, he placed the police battalion and the 2nd Livno Brigade in the same context, which he should not have, because that was not the case. The Livno Brigade is one thing, and the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police was a military unit and was not on the strength of the Petar Kresimir IV Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me just ask a question to what you've just said in clarification. So you said that one of the things you reported here is that the commander of the Professional Battalion -- let me first ask: Was this name Mr. Goran Vucica; is that correct? Do you recall whether that was his name?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, the name is Vucica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What you report is the following: You say that Mr. Vucica said that you had received an order to reconnoiter the field from Mr. Coric, so was he wrong when he said that? Did you receive an order from Coric to reconnoiter the field or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Vucica did not receive an order from Mr. Coric, because Mr. Coric was not his superior, and he spoke on behalf of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You misunderstand me, because what Mr. Vucica is saying, not that he received an order from Coric, but that you had received an order from Coric to reconnoiter the field. And my question is: Is that correct? Had you received an order from Mr. Coric; not Mr. Vucica, but you?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we did not receive an order. Mr. Vucica, to cover himself, he said that we had received that order from Coric, and that is simply not the case. It's a lie. And that was the cause of the argument, because Vucica had lied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that Mr. Vucica left as a result of this quarrel, that he left Prozor with his Professional Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. A follow-up question on this document. You have said, Mr. Andabak, that the military did not have the authority to name or remove members of the police. Here, apparently, Mr. Praljak threatened to dismiss you. Was he entitled to dismiss you? Could he have done this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he could have instituted the proceedings for my dismissal, but he is a very short-tempered person. Whenever he faced an opposition, that's how he reacted. He threatened all of us to dismiss us, to replace us; not just me, but with everybody, even my commander with whom he argued quite often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. This does not sound entirely unbelievable, having had observed Mr. Praljak. Could one say, generally, that he was not very enthusiastic about rules and respecting rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you may be right in putting it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first of all, there is a small mistake in the English translation. There is a date, the 20th of July. It's actually the 29th of July, isn't it? Witness, on the 29th of July, General Praljak reported as Chief of Staff. And immediately after taking up this position, he uses his new powers by deciding to attack this location. And the handwritten report that you drafted, because I believe this was a handwritten report, this report states that General Praljak had given you an order; and, therefore, you had to abide by this order, regardless of the fact that you could also report to Mr. Coric. I was wondering whether you received a response from Mr. Coric after handing this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just explain. The order that was issued by General Praljak, the 2nd Light Assault Battalion did go to reconnoiter in Duratbegov Dolac and remain there, unlike the Professional Battalion that returned, and that was on the 27th. And we reported to Mr. Coric on the 29th in order to complain against General Praljak and General Milenko Filipovic, who didn't behave properly and used inappropriate expressions and words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did Mr. Coric respond or not to you, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't remember. Very well. This is all I wanted to know. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly warn the witness that if he has the same word in one sentence, he has to speak much slower because his words are being lost in translation, and it will help both the transcriber and the interpreters. I've been following the transcript, and I can see the trouble looming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, please try to slow down. You speak very quickly. I do the same. We speak very fast, so please try and slow down when you take the floor. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you to look at the next document, which is P03821. It's the next one in the binder. And this is, in fact, a report from Mr. Vucica to his superior about what happened when he had this meeting with Mr. Andabak -- with Mr. Praljak. And, again, I won't read out the whole report, but I will read segments from the report in order to get an impression on what his view was. Starting with the second paragraph of the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the interruption. Before you start reading, I didn't want to interrupt you before, I have an objection to the interpretation of one word which I believe is very important. On page 8, line 5, the witness was answering Judge Trechsel's first question and said, about Praljak: [In English] "Your Honour, he could have instituted the proceedings for my dismissal." [Interpretation] And that's how it was recorded. I'm not sure that that corresponds to the witness's words. I am not sure that the word "instituted" actually corresponds with the word the witness used. He said that he could have started or initiated or gave a proposal for the dismissal. That was the sense of the verb that the witness used. I checked the word "instituted" in the dictionary in the meantime, and the word "instituted" means that he had the right to institute, and he didn't have that right. He had the right to initiate the proceedings, and this is an entirely different thing. Since we're talking about a very delicate matter, I would kindly ask you to clarify with the witness and ask him what he meant when he said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that General Praljak could initiate the proceedings to lead -- leading to the establishment of my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, since we've clarified that, let's now look at P03821, and I'll read out a couple of paragraphs from this document, the report from Mr. Vucica. Starting with the second paragraph: "On the same evening at 2300 hours, I personally, together with Mr. Aldo Delic, deputy commander of the battalion, met with Mr. Praljak and Mr. Filipovic at the Zone of Operations Headquarters, where I was supposed to receive instructions and further orders. During the issuing of orders by Mr. Praljak and Mr. Filipovic, I have noticed a lot of illogical remarks and the lack of knowledge about the situation on the ground." And then moving to the bottom of the page in the English version and to the top of the page in the B/C/S version, the top of the next page: "I went to the Vakuf Operations Centre together with Aldo Delic, deputy commander, and Zdenko Andabak, MP commander from Livno, to get initial information. There, I received the first true and good information, and I met people who were drawing the enemy positions on the map located in the Zone of Operations in Prozor. All my suspicions with regards to the enemy artillery pieces, for which General Praljak and Mr. Filipovic told me that did not exist, proved to be true." Moving down to the second paragraph -- moving down two paragraphs: "After carrying out reconnaissance, I, together with Mr. Andabak, reported to Mr. Praljak and informed him on everything and suggested again that the action be postponed and planned in detail." And then the next paragraph: "At my persistent insistence that the meeting of the OZ command and all commanders who have arrived at Prozor with their units be held, and that the overall and the detailed plan be made, I was faced with the disregard and insulting by Mr. Praljak and his rejection of information that I have obtained on the ground. Mr. Andabak was also not spared from the threats and insults. Upon analysing the overall situation, that is, the misinformation that I was faced with, the ignorance of the command staff, its complete refusal of anybody's advice or remarks, I have decided to take the unit back to Livno." Now, sir, Mr. Vucica has no good words for the professional skills of General Praljak, to say the least, and also of Commander Filipovic. Do you share his opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I spent a lot of time with General Praljak in the field. I knew his character and nature, I knew his position, I knew that he was a temperamental person and he swore a lot. And I don't think that General Filipovic, who was from Livno, could influence -- I agree that he could do that, and that may not have been professional, but when it comes to General Praljak's temperament, since I knew him in the field, I knew how he behaved, when he uttered those insults and threats, I found that normal. And here Mr. Vucica considers me the commander of the military police. However, I was there only as the assistant chief of the MP Administration, and it was Mr. Jasarevic who received orders, and he was the commander of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You talk about Mr. Praljak's temperament, and we all know about Mr. Praljak's temperament, but here the report goes a bit further. It talks about lack of knowledge on the situation on the ground, and the thing is you seem, at least from your own report, to have agreed with Mr. Vucica that at the time there was need for more troops and that, you know, the operation shouldn't have started. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, I agree with that. So I never went into the operations, I always -- without doing the necessary preparations. I would always see to that beforehand so that the attack could be a good-quality one and to see that we could keep casualties down to a minimum. But Goran Vucica before this time, and that's what I'd like to tell you, lost some men on another front, in another battleground, and so he was frightened, he had this fear. So I don't know what his position was, but, anyway, he went back to Livno. He didn't want to go out on assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at one more document on this topic, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, this document sheds a lot of light for a Judge on the atmosphere within the HVO. We can see that the Chief of Staff gives an order and that the order is not executed, because Goran Vucica leaves. We can see that the information given to General Praljak was serious information; in other words, the enemy had artillery pieces, which General Praljak did not want to consider. It's a shame he is not here today. He is not here today because he feels that he is not being given the fair trial he is entitled to. That is why he's not here today. I'm sure that if he had been here today, he would have paid attention to this document, which I'm sure reminded him of a particular event. What I would like to know is this: When you receive an order, even if this order is nonsensical, do you need to execute it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I were to be given that kind of order, I would carry it out, but I would always inform the Military Police Administration about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to know. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In follow-up on this, I think the next exhibit is going to be interesting. It's Exhibit 5D04094, probably at the back of the binder. 5D04094. Now, sir, as you can see, this is a communication from Mr. Coric to Mr. Praljak, and it's dated the 31st of July. And it reads: "I was informed by the commander of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion, Mr. Muamir Jasarevic, on the position of the units in Pavic Polje. "By detailed analysis of the situation, we propose emergent strengthening of the position and preventing Muslim forces while attempting to surround the 2nd Light Assault Battalion. We are kindly asking you to do everything in order to prevent that civilians and soldiers in this village stay surrounded." Now, sir, would you agree with me here that Mr. Coric is exerting his direct influence over the operations of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion by forwarding this communication to General Praljak, and that he knew exactly what went on there?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know what the command of the Light Assault Battalion wrote to Mr. Coric in his report, but obviously the report was not favourable to the 2nd Light Assault Battalion which was in Pavic Polje, and I don't think that Valentin Coric had any influence or could wield any influence. He just informed General Praljak that he had received information of some kind and that the situation wasn't a good one. He didn't go further than that. Now, whether it was up to General Praljak or the person whom he designated to check this out to see what the situation was actually like on the ground, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But he had received the information about that; is that -- would you agree that Mr. Coric was informed by the commander of the position of the 2nd Light Assault? Does that surprise you, that the commander went to Mr. Coric to inform him about his position?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, just as I was assistant chief -- so the commander of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion attended briefings at the forward command post of the operative zone, and he would be given assignments: And the commander of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion in that place, Pavic Polje, he was there alone, encircled, under siege, and so he informed Mr. Coric about that. He told him where he was and that he was in a difficult position. And it seems that nobody took his plight seriously in the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Coric, let me remind you that, normally speaking, your counsel will have time for redirect and that you are going to testify. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I assume that my Defence counsel will be able to respond with a document, by presenting a document that came back before my one. But as we're under time constraints, I'm not sure whether she has prepared the document. But my counsel says she has prepared it, so everything will be revealed in due course when my counsel responds. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, just one last question on this document. Would you agree with me that Mr. Coric was issuing this document because he felt responsible for the soldiers of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, yes, certainly, just like any member of the military police if they were in danger. He was supposed to -- he should have expressed his condolences to the family and said, Your son has died, and he could have prevented something, perhaps; not him, personally, but like with this letter, to prevent the event from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's move to another document and another topic. Could I ask you to look at Exhibit P07553. Now, sir, this document is an order from you, dated the 11th of January, 1994, and it's based on an order from Siljeg on the improvement supervision of movement and transport of persons and motor vehicles bearing HV insignia. And in this order, you order: "To immediately take all necessary measures of increased supervision while conducting patrol service and control at check-points for the purpose of timely identification of persons and motor vehicles which bear insignia indicating their affiliation with the Croatian Army." And, secondly: "Identify all persons, taking all required information on them, with the obligation to immediately remove the mentioned insignia, and if they refuse to do so, bring them into custody into the official premises of the military police units." And: "The same procedure is to be applied to motor vehicles." Now, sir, do you recall issuing this order, and why was it necessary to immediately remove HV insignia on persons and motor vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I really couldn't answer that. This is the first time that I see this document, and my deputy commander has signed it, as far as I can see. His name was Blazenko Bodulusic. So he issued orders according to the orders issued to him by the Military Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying even though your name is written there, it's somebody else's signature, and you don't know about this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see. So I don't know anything about this document, in actual fact, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's move on, then. Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Colonel, this document lies at the heart of the Prosecution case. As regards the international armed conflict and the intervention of the Republic of Croatia in the conflict, someone reading this document may have two views on it: A, the person issuing this order does not know that there is an agreement between Tudjman and Boban on the involvement of the Croatian Army, and, therefore, thinks that it is un-normal for foreign vehicles to be circulated. Therefore, your subordinate abides by this order to prevent this. That could be one point of view. B, second point of view, as the HVO knows that the international community is observing what is going on on all sides, the UNPROFOR, seeing a Croatian Army vehicle circulate with identification of units and registration number plates, could report to Kiseljak and say that the Croatian Army is in Herzegovina. Therefore, you in the HVO, you're trying to conceal the presence of the Croatian Army by controlling things in this manner. There are two points of view or two ways of reading this document. The Judges, of course, when they deliberate confidentially, will address this issue, but we haven't reached that stage yet. You will, perhaps, help us take our decision when the time comes. What does this document mean, do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I can tell you now, looking at this order, is that we didn't want -- or, rather, the HVO -- or the Croatian people in Herceg-Bosna didn't want to hide the presence. Well, what you said first. We wanted to prevent it. Now, had we wanted to hide something, then everything would be kept to an oral level. There wouldn't be any documents. And individual HVO members, on occasion, would receive, from their relatives who were in the Croatian Army and in the Croatian police force, uniforms with insignia, with HV insignia or some HV unit insignia, so that led to misunderstandings too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's gain some time. Let me finish off my question, and then my colleague will intervene. We are on the 11th of January, 1994. Under oath, can you tell me, as far as you know, whether the Croatian Army was in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina during this period or not? My question is very clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, and we can only speak about General Filipovic -- now, that the complete Croatian Army was there, no, it wasn't, but General Filipovic came in from the area of Tomislavgrad, which is where his parents lived and where he was born, so that perhaps he brought in some experience gained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, an answer you have given a short while ago does not appear very convincing to me. You said there was nothing to hide, as a comment -- an order to remove insignia, because if one wanted to hide something, one would not create documents. Now, insignia, it's even contained in the term, are visible. They are -- they show to everyone who comes across, whereas these document, of course -- this order was certainly not published in the newspaper, so it was not public. And I do not think that -- I wonder how you can explain the fact that there was an order demanding the removal of insignia shows that there was nothing to hide. To me, this does not quite infringe, I would say, "ca cloche."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then my deputy commander in that case would most probably have received an oral order to implement the order, but without any papers, no trace, no trace of anything happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, just one follow-up question on one of the answers you gave to the Judges. You were saying: "As far as I remember, and we can only speak about General Filipovic -- now, that the complete Croatian Army was there, no, it wasn't." When you say -- does that imply that certain segments of the Croatian Army were there? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was about the Croatian Army. All I said -- and I thought that meant the whole army. I said that as far as I know, the people from the Croatian Army who were there, somebody who came frequently was General Filipovic, but he originated from our region and not as was stated in the question, the Croatian Army as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're now referring to one person, but could it have been that there were certain units of the Croatian Army, or you don't know that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I knew that Mr. Filipovic came with two or three squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where was this in Central Bosnia, in which region? Is that the region we just discussed, Gornji Vakuf and Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's move to another topic which -- we'll go back to Livno. Sir, is it correct that around the 21st of July, 1993, that armed clashes broke out between the Muslims and the Croats in Livno?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I think on Monday you testified that following these clashes, you received an order from the brigade commander to disarm, arrest, and detain all the Muslim men of military age in Livno; is that correct? Was that following these armed clashes that you received that order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the military police and the brigade, the Petar Kresimir IV Brigade. From the brigade commander, that's where the order came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So do you recall approximately how many Muslim men in Livno were arrested and detained on that occasion? Can you give an approximate figure?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if I were to give you an exact figure, I would be lying. I know that they were people from the age of 18 to 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you about an exact figure, but an approximate figure. Are we talking about hundreds, are we talking about thousands? Could you give an approximate figure?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to speculate. Whatever I say would not be right, so I don't want to put myself into a position like that whereby I was asked to quote figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Fair enough, fair enough. I won't insist. But is it correct, and I think you testified to that, that these men, you know, they were detained for only a couple of days, and after that they were allowed to go home again; is that correct? I think that's what you testified on Monday.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. So they were detained for two to three days, a maximum of two to three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you were asked by the Coric counsel if there was any prison in Livno in 1993, you, in fact, stated: "No, I would say -- I would say -- I would not say that there was a prison in 1993. I would say it was more of a collection centre which existed as a place where disarmed Muslims were taken and stayed there for three to five days, depending on their role in their armed uprisal against the Croats." That's what you testified to on Monday.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and that's what I said. And I stand by that. It wasn't a classical prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit P03716. I think this document was also shown to you before. Yesterday, I think yesterday. And it's a report from the assistant chief for security, Tucak, and it's addressed to Mr. Coric, and it's dated the 26th of July, 1993. Now, I'll just read out the second paragraph, which I'm interested in, and which reads -- no, I'm sorry: "The 2nd Light Assault Battalion and the 2nd Battalion, 2nd Company, about 1600 people were detained in total, and 1.000 of them have already been set free. 166 people were detained in the Zabrisce school because they refused to surrender and offered armed resistance. The remaining prisoners are held in the gym of the Livno elementary school. One of the detainees is a religious official." Now, sir, is it correct that this document actually reports about what we've just said, the general disarmament of the Muslim men in Livno?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please? I'm note sure I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We just said that after the clashes on the 21st of July, there was a general disarmament and arrest of all the Muslim men of military age, so my question is, in fact: Is this a report of what happened when the operation occurred? It says here that 1600 people were detained. Does this actually refer to the round-up of the Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that's the operation, but let me say that Branimir Tucak, as assistant chief of the Military Police Administration for security, he received all this information from the assistant commander of the Livno Brigade for SIS. The military police had nothing to do with this kind of report, nor did it have any other activities linked to detention or collection centres and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this report says that 1600 people were detained and thousands of them were already set free. What about the 1600 other detainees who were kept in these various detention centres? Did they remain in detention or were they also released?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, Mr. Prosecutor, because already on the 27th of July -- or, rather, that night, the night between the 26th and the 27th, pursuant to an order by General Praljak that we talked about a moment ago, we went on assignment to Gornji Vakuf, so that I don't know. Everything was conducted by the Livno Brigade with respect to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, sir, you say you don't know, but on Monday you were very adamant in saying that people were not imprisoned in Livno and that after this operation everyone was released again. How can you -- how could you state that so sure if you now say that you weren't there and you don't know what happened with these other 600 people?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I repeat what I said on Monday. I know I have information -- I received information that people were detained for two to three days, and then they were released and allowed to go home. The armed conflict in Livno took place on the 23rd of July, and this is a report dated the 26th of July, so I don't see how that changes anything and how it's different from my statement. That's what I said to begin with; people went home. Now, who interrogated these people, the ones who offered resistance, and there was an armed conflict, we weren't there and we weren't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that on the 13th of August, 1993, that there was another order issued by the Chief of the Main Staff to arrest 132 Muslim men from Livno who were identified by the SIS as Muslim extremists? Let's have a look at Exhibit P04228, which maybe will refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, let's look at the next document. But I have taken my calculating machine. 1.600 detained, a thousand released, so there are 600 left. 166 opposed an armed resistance and were detained in the Zabrisce school. 334 are unaccounted for. The Prosecutor says that the SIS arrested 130 people afterwards, so I don't know whether these 132 must be included in the figure of 334 or whether one should add them on to the figure. Whatever the case may be, on the basis of the document I have before me, I have the feeling that all the people who were arrested were either interrogated by the SIS or by the military police. As far as you know -- this is my question. My question is a lengthy question, because I set everything against the backdrop of what happened so that you are able to understand my question. This is my question: According to you, all the people who were arrested, were they automatically interrogated either by the SIS or by the military police, as part of investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, SIS interrogated only those who were known to have actively prepared the organised attack on HVO in Livno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the military police; what did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the military police was one of the units under the command of the brigade during the conflict and during the subsequent disarmament. The Crime Prevention Department of the Military Police got involved at the moment when two MPs were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to look at Exhibit P04228. I don't know if you already found it or not, 4228. It's a report from you, addressed to Coric, dated the 16th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I be assisted with finding the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: P4228, P4228. You can see it on the screen. There we have it. So as I said, this is a report from you to Mr. Coric, and it refers to an order of the Chief of the Main Staff, dated the 13th of August, and, in fact, that order is attached to this document. There's two documents attached to this one, a list of 132 names and then the actual order from the Main Staff which was signed by Mr. -- by Brigadier Tole. So just to read out the first paragraph: "On 14 August 1993, we began implementing the order of the chief of the HVO Main Staff, and according to the list compiled by the SIS of the Petar Kresimir Brigade from Livno, a total of 132 Muslims have been taken into custody for whom there are reasonable grounds to suspect that they participated in the clashes between the Croats and the Muslims on the 21st of July, 1993, in Livno, and spread Muslim fundamentalism." So is it correct that these 132 Muslims were arrested on the basis of this order from the Main Staff, dated the 13th of August?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an objection. I apologise to my learned friend, Mr. Bos. Maybe it was an unintentional mistake. This document by Zarko Tole is not an order. It was sent to Mr. Coric. Zarko Tole was not authorised to issue orders to the chief of the Military Police Administration, and if you have a closer look at this, you'll see it is a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I'm reacting to the qualification according to which this is an order by the Chief of the Main Staff, and I'm drawing your attention to the fact that this document is not an order. I don't have any other objections. This is simply not an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It says "Zapovjed" in Croatian and "Order" in English, so, I mean, you may perhaps have another opportunity to react, but I think this is -- or I have the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document was signed by Zarko Tole, but that document does not contain the word "Zapovjed."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I think all the documentation is here. We have the document from Mr. Andabak where the subject writes -- it refers to the order of the Chief of the Main Staff, and we also have the document, itself, which apparently doesn't say "Order," so we can all see -- we can all draw our conclusions from the documents. All the documents are here. Maybe I'll have to repeat what I just said. Still no translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I think there is no B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It works now, there is translation? One, two, three. Is there a B/C/S translation? Well, Your Honours, we seem to have a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'll try another mike.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, and I, of course, looked at what I had before me, and that was only the other one in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's okay now, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that all channels are working now. I have checked, and I can hear the B/C/S booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So what I said is all the documents are here, and I think, you know, the issue has now been solved. So we have everything in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you -- my question to you was: Were these 132 Muslims, in fact, arrested in Livno as a result of this -- well, this document which you have referred to as the order of the Chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. The Livno Brigade could not carry out the task on its own, with its own brigade military police. They requested for the active-duty military police to get involved, and that was done. I believe that the commander of the Petar Kresimir IV Brigade gave me this document from General Tole, and in my report I enclosed the order of the Chief of the Main Staff to illustrate the behaviour and the conduct of the military police, as well as a list of the detained persons, and I copied all that to Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, were these 132 prisoners, were they considered as prisoners of war, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know how the SIS of the brigade portrayed them or listed them. In any case, they were soldiers of the HVO of Muslim ethnicity. They had organised and planned the attack. I don't know how they listed them. Our task was to assist with bringing them in and handing them over to the brigade SIS. I repeat, we did not engage in any other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know how long these people remained in detention?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Prosecutor, they stayed there for a very short time. I believe that only one person from that group, close to the top echelons of the SDA and one of the organisers of that resistance, as far as I heard from the brigade, that person requested to be relocated to a third country for his own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying "a very short time." Are we talking a few days, a few weeks, a few months? Could you be a bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I ask you now to look at Exhibit P09668. 9668. Well, while the usher is trying to find the document, let me just say that this is an ECMM document dated the 24th of September, 1993, and it reports on a visit to the HVO headquarters, the imam, and the military police in Livno. Sir, let me first draw your attention to item number 2 of this report, which says, you know, that the ECMM delegation -- it says: "We had a meeting with the HVO commanders of the Livno Brigade, and we have noted the following statements:" And then they list three statements. Do you have it? Maybe the usher could help to find the B/C/S version. We're looking at -- so we're looking at item number 2, Colonel, which is entitled "Political Situation." So it says that this ECMM delegation met with the HVO commanders of the Livno brigade, and then they noted a couple of statements that these people made. And the third one says: "When the Muslims and Bosnian Serbs want to live in this country, they have to obey their rules." Meaning, you know, the Croatian rules. Sir, was that a general feeling among the Croatians in Livno, that the Muslims and the Bosnian Serbs had to obey by the rules of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, let me just correct you. As far as I know, this delegation had a separate meeting with me and a separate one with Mr. Jasarevic. As far as the political situation was concerned, I wouldn't agree with this. I don't know who told them that. Maybe they drew their own conclusions based on their own views.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. So you wouldn't agree. Let's move, then, to paragraph number 4, and this talks about the humanitarian situation. And it reads: "We had a meeting with the imam of Livno, and we got the following information: Most of the Muslims of Livno want to stay in Livno, although at this moment the times are difficult for them. After the clashes in Bugojno started the provocations, meetings, robberies, closing of shops, against the Muslims started in Livno, at 21 July 1993. Now the provocations has decreased, but the Muslims are still afraid." The last sentence of this paragraph: "In Livno, there are approximately 200 to 300 Muslim POWs (imprisoned soldiers in a school, 100 to 150) in garages and the building of the civilian police." Now, sir, it talks here about 200 to 300 Muslim prisoners of war, and you just testified that, you know -- that most of the Muslims who -- you know, who were arrested stayed for two to three days in detention and then were released again. Would this be a false information that has been given here about the 200 to 300 Muslim POWs? And this is a report from late 1993, so it's about, you know, more than a month after the 13 August arrests.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know. He may be just throwing figures just like that, improvising. I could have also told you that 300 or 400 Muslims were arrested in Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying that this is not correct, that there weren't 200 to 300 Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, are you referring to the imam's statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm just asking you. If I were to say, Were there 200 to 300 Muslim detainees in Livno on the 24th of September, 1993, would you say that that is correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that I don't know. Whatever I would have told you, I would lie [as interpreted]. All these questions should be put to the Livno Brigade. I was not in Livno all that time. Therefore, there's no way I could know whether there were or whether there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- let's move on, and let me read to you the third paragraph of item number 4, and I'll read it out: "Suddenly, the above-mentioned meeting with the imam was disturbed by crying women who entered the imam's office. They tried to explain us that just a few minutes ago POWs at the school were beaten and there was many blood. We should go with them to the school. The military police who were escorting us took us to the office of the military police. The head of the second unit, Zdenko Andabak, and a Muslim member, Muamir Jasarevic of the military police, explained to us that there were no problems and we can go visit the POWs in the school, but first we had to go to the security officer from HVO. We did, and unfortunately he was on the terrain. When we went back to Tomislavgrad, we were blocked at the HVO check-point. They accused us of taking photos, which we didn't. After discussions and many talks, we were allowed to travel to Tomislavgrad. "Comment: We have got the impression that they have misled us and that they were thinking we have seen too much." Now, sir, it appears from reading this -- it's not very clear, but it appears that the ECMM delegation eventually could not visit the prisoners of -- the POWs in the school because this HVO security officer was not present but was somewhere on the terrain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know whether that is correct or not. I don't know whether they could be visited or not. The military police -- the active-duty military police, including the 2nd Light Assault and the 6th Battalions, had nothing whatsoever to do with the persons of Muslim ethnicity in Livno, when it came to guarding them, taking them away, or anything else. And when the International Monitors say that military policemen came and escorted them, those were brigade military policemen, and that's why I told them, every time they wanted permission to do something, to go to the brigade SIS, and it would be the SIS of the brigade who would be able to inform them about the numbers of the people who were kept in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, sir, your name is specifically mentioned in this report, and I'm just asking you about this specific ECMM visit. And you seem to recall that these people came to visit. So on this particular incident, did the ECMM delegation eventually get into the school? Can you give an answer to that? They had spoken with you, and you went with them to the school? Did they get into the school or not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've just explained. My headquarters was not even close to school. It was at the far end of the town. And I told them -- I told the brigade military policemen to take them to the brigade. A member of that mission thought that we were the military police and that we were in charge of those Muslims, but I'm telling you that we were not at all in any connection with those people. That's why I told them to go to the brigade, to the brigade SIS. I was not authorised to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bos, you've run out of time, so please use the credit of 30 seconds to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I have my 30 seconds left, I would just want to finish with one last document, and that's Exhibit P06867.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If you could look at -- that's going to be the last document I'm going to show you, Witness, P06867. Sir, this is an SIS report from the Petar Kresimir Brigade, and it's a report on you. It's dated the 25th of November, 1993. And I can't read out the whole report, but I'm going to read out one segment, and then we'll be finished with this cross-examination. I'll start with the English translation on the bottom of page 1. It says: "It's important to emphasise that public in Livno knew all about his military merits, and that is why Zdenko Andabak was soon in the public eye. We also have to emphasise that some soldiers who, along with him, carried out tasks and duties from the beginning, don't like him. One part of the public objects the fact that he owns quite a few luxurious and expensive cars and jeeps. He's criticised for driving in 30 such cars after the operation in Prozor in December 1992. He's also reproached for disturbing the public on several occasions, for shooting, willful interventions in civilian life, willful violations of regulations on curfew, patronising certain catering facilities, usurping facilities of Livno police departments, special-task units, and accepting into the unit policemen with undeniable criminal leaning. "One part of members from the 2nd Light Assault Battalion is from Bugojno. Later status show there was 90 of them, and they show a tendency to be involved in numerous criminal and illegal activities, primarily the violence against Muslims, forceful entering into apartments, illegal commandeering of cars, et cetera. Zdenko Andabak is reproached for doing almost nothing in that area, although having significant influence over the 2nd Light Assault Battalion policemen. "When comparing these two different characteristics, it's necessary to differentiate all Zdenko Andabak's achievements at the battle-field and his other qualities." Sir, isn't this SIS report an accurate reflection of your conduct during the war; that you were a successful MP commander in combat operations, but at the same time you allowed soldiers under your command to commit war crimes against the Muslims and you were personally involved in the looting of property?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, whatever has just been read out and what has been written is a lie. I know the author of this text personally. Therefore, if anybody prevented anything from happening in Livno, it was me. Whenever you want, you can come and check with the Muslims and with the Serbs to hear from them what the military police did for them. After the disarmament, when I asked for all Bosniak bars and property to be protected, when the president of the municipality came and when I told him what I was doing, or when I asked him what he was doing, everybody thought that he was trying to engage in a putsch, and he mentioned some professional policemen. He says that Tomislav Garic is acting against the interests of the Croats. I had over my head of the turbo Ustashas [as interpreted] everything is a lie, starting with my CV, where I was born, where I was educated, where I came from. He should have checked better. And as for him, about this official who wrote this report, I could easily write a novel about him. And if I have done anything, Your Honours, I am an officer of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the nucleus of the Armed Forces of BH components were composed of the military policemen under my command or under the command of different people in my area of responsibility, and I am proud of my work. It is always the military police that are blamed for everything, without proper verification, without proper checking of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bos. We will have our first break, as every Thursday, and we will resume for Mr. Coric's Defence. The time that you have used for -- that you will be able to use for redirect will be deducted from your overall credit of time that has been allocated to you. We agree, don't we? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that we will not need a lot of time for additional questions, so I believe we will be able to finish earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll break as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Before I give the floor to Mr. Coric's Defence counsel for her redirect, I would like to read out an oral decision which will supplement what I said a while ago, after Mr. Stewart's intervention, for things to be quite clear. Oral decision clarifying the decision handed down at the beginning of this hearing relating to D4's application to file extra motions pursuant to Guide-line 9. At the beginning of today's hearing, the Petkovic Defence asked the Trial Chamber leave to file motions relating to the tendering of extra exhibits, the status of which is currently pending before the Trial Chamber. In light of a good administration of justice, and to avoid too many written submissions, the Trial Chamber would like to ask the Petkovic Defence to file a single motion, pursuant to Guide-line 9, at the latest by the 22nd of March, 2010, and to include in this motion all the documents which are the subject of this pending motion before the Trial Chamber. In other words, if there are some exhibits on which the Trial Chamber has not ruled yet because the witnesses have already been heard, and you have asked for these exhibits to be tendered, and these have been given IC numbers, this means that by the 22nd of March, in this single motion, all these exhibits should be mentioned, which means that afterwards, if the Trial Chamber hands down a decision or is of a view to admitting an exhibit at a witness's hearing -- let me repeat. If an exhibit is mentioned in a pending motion, and if the Trial Chamber admits this exhibit at the time the Trial Chamber hands down its decision on the motion pursuant to Guide-line 9, the Trial Chamber will specify that it is moot. If, however, the exhibit has been dismissed in the pending motion, when the time comes for the Trial Chamber to review the single motion of the 22nd of March, 2010, the Trial Chamber can then, if the need arises, admit this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for that explanation. Now, since the Petkovic Defence, towards the end of its documentary evidence motion in which it included the documents which were not put forward through a witness, and we compiled our motion on the basis of your decisions thus far, Your Honours, and the conditions under which the other Defenses prepared their documentary evidence motion, we have to accept your ruling, of course, by which you're changing what has been the practice so far, and there's no problem in that regard. But in that case, I would like to request that you extend our dead-line so that instead of the 22nd of March, we can file our motion by the end of next week, which is Friday, I believe, the 27th of March. No, the 26th of March. I apologise. So in that case, could you allow us that extra time to file our motion, as we have conceived it, by the end of business on the 26th of March? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber grants your application for additional time. Mr. Coric's Defence counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom. Re-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, Mr. Andabak. I'm going to start from where the Prosecution left off. And before I ask my introductory question, may we have Prosecution document P06867 up on e-court, please. And the Judges should have it in the binder. It's the last document shown by the Prosecutor. And, Mr. Andabak, you said, of this document, when commenting about what you thought of its contents and the person compiling the report, that you had had enough of these, what you called, turbo Ustashas. Now, I'd like to read out certain portions of this report that the Prosecutor did not read out, and you didn't have enough time to read it out yourself, to see what this person criticised you of. So let's look at page 2. It's both page 2 of the English and the Croatian. It says: "The public was irritated when, for an official cameraman of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion, Hajrudin Terzic was named, a Muslim from Livno, the owner of a video-tech and a film amateur -- a life-long film amateur was appointed official cameraman, when we know his political past and his political orientation, and the role of his father in the elimination of the Croats from Livno, members of the Ustasha Home Guards units." And then a few lines down it says the following: "Part of the public did not agree at all with the appointment of Tomislav Garic as security officer within the unit, considering the fact that his past is also known, and his characteristics -- character traits are not at all commendable, and also his attitude towards Croatian-hood." And towards the end of the document, on the last page, three paragraphs from the end, there's a sentence that reads as follows: "The details for which this is being called up are appointing Muamir Jasarevic, Babo," who is a Muslim, "as commander of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion." Now, you mentioned these Ustashas, which you called "turbo Ustashas." Are these the kind of characteristics that you associate with these men?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel. They are great Croats or Croats that caused the greatest problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andabak. Now, I was struck by a name I saw there about Mr. Vucica. Document P03821, a person by the name of Aldo Delic is mentioned there. Was that a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, Aldo Delic was a member -- or, rather, a deputy -- Vucica's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he a Muslim too?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I don't know that. I don't know how he declared himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think you've received the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am reluctant to intervene during the redirect, but when something important arises, I do. It's the first time I hear the term "great Croats." Can you very briefly tell me what this means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they were people who, before the war, were members of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and afterwards -- or, rather, during the war, in the course of the war, they returned to their Catholic faith, if we're talking about the Croats. And they would go to church every Sunday, sitting in the first pew, and then they would persecute those who were going about their jobs honourably because they wanted to prove themselves and atone for their sins, the sins they had committed during the Communist system, Communist rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, you have two sets of documents in front of you, and we're going to look at the first set with just two documents. And the first document is 5D04094. I have put that document in there to jog your memory, refresh your memory. It was one that the Prosecutor showed you. It is Mr. Coric's request, sent to Mr. Praljak, linked to the situation in Pavic Polje. And you said on that occasion -- or, rather, earlier on you said that Mr. Coric felt himself responsible because he would be the one who, if those soldiers happened to be killed, would have to go and express his condolences to their families. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, which is 5D04092. And this document is signed by the duty officer of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion of the Military Police. It is sent to Mr. Coric. The date is the 30th of July, the day before the document that we looked at a moment ago. And the subject is -- well, it says "Report/Request," "Re. Report/Request." And in the document, it says as follows: "On the 29th of July, 1993, at around 1100 hours, we received through Paket link a request from Mr. Zdenko Andabak for assistance in both men and materiel MTS. "He is currently in Pavic Polje and is in danger of being encircled." And now it goes on to say what they need urgently, and then finally it says: "This is all the information we have at the moment. It is possible that the above Paket communication was the last communication with them. Please assess the situation and do everything in your power." Mr. Andabak, the document we saw from Mr. Coric a moment ago, was that a response to the request that we're looking at on our screens now? Is that what that was?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go back to the beginning of the cross-examination and start off with the Praljak Defence and address those issues. The Praljak Defence asked you, on cross-examination, about re-subordination of the military police to the commanders of the HVO. Do you remember that, that you were questioned about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at the first document. It's in English, and I'll read it out. It is P10029, and it is an excerpt, the part that I'm going to read out, from the testimony of Mr. Petkovic in the Kordic trial. What I'm going to read out is to be found on pages 26820, lines 2 to 5 and 10 to 16. I'll read it out in English, and you listen: [In English] "Not only on the 14th of April, but a long time prior to that, ever since the establishment of the 4th Military Police Battalion, it was under the authority of the operative zone and, therefore, under his command." My first question: Mr. Andabak, the 4th Battalion of the Military Police was in which operation zone? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection. Could my learned friend tell us to which part of the cross-examination is she referring so as to enable us to find that part in the transcript and see whether these questions, indeed, concern the cross-examination. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can do it; no problem. I did -- I could make an introduction, but I didn't want to suggest the witness what I'm going to talk to him about. The Praljak Defence, throughout the entire cross-examination on the first day of the cross-examination, was showing the gentleman some orders about the re-subordination of the MP battalions. And based on that, they drew conclusions that without those orders, the military police would not have been re-subordinated to the OZ commander. Just a moment, please. Let me finish. Those were orders that concerned -- I can read all the documents, if necessary, but then I would be quoting the cross-examination of Mr. Kovacic. But there were at least 10 orders which all, to the last, concerned one principal and one situation. And if I'm allowed to put my first question or my first two questions to the witness, after establishing that the witness knows what this is about, for the -- I could ask the witness to leave the courtroom to explain to everybody what I'm going to be doing during my additional questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In cross-examination of Mr. Andabak, I did not step out of the OZ North-West Bosnia -- or, rather, Herzegovina, save for one part when I mentioned South-East Herzegovina. I did not deal with facts, documents, and events in Central Bosnia, and I have a reason for that. And if you want me to do so, I can explain. And I have to say this because the OZ under Blaskic's command in Central Bosnia, when it came to the organisation and relationship between the HVO and the military police, was an exception to the rule because they were isolated, and this was obviously the subject of my cross-examination and the document that my learned friend has just provided. I would like to object, and I state that my learned friend is now leaving the area of my cross-examination. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not about the area. I'm trying to show the principle, and I'm not going to go out of North-West Herzegovina, nor am I going to ask the witness about the OZ Central Bosnia. But if I'm allowed to put my questions, then I will entertain all the objections if they believe that my questions are not fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Even the first question here, she is quoting from Petkovic's transcript in Kordic about Central Bosnia. That's where he was asked about Central Bosnia, and the situation there was not identical, in terms of establishment, in terms of agreements, in terms of different documents, as in the other operations zones. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'm going to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I'll respond to Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Kovacic, that's your position. That's not the same. Perhaps the witness will agree with you. Let's just wait and see. All the more reason to wait. Put your question, and we'll see afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. I have an objection to the objections of this kind because Mr. Kovacic is testifying. He is making decisions as to what we have seen in what operations zone, and I don't think it's fair, especially in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I picked him up on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to take up any more of your time, but I have to object to my learned friend's words. I'm not testifying, I've never testified. I'm not prepared to engage in this discussion in these proceedings. Documents have been seen. Mr. Petkovic has spoken about that. Mr. Praljak has spoken about that. There is plenty of evidence in this case that the situation is different in Central Bosnia than Herzegovina. But it was not my intention to explain how the situation differed. That would have been testifying. I just said that she could not compare apples and oranges. That was my point that I was making. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] If this is not testifying, if this is not testifying, then I'm going to say that these are not apples and pears, but just apples, and then we will move on to a different thing. And I'm going to remind the witness what I read. I read that from the setting-up of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, that 4th Battalion was under the command of the operations zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really, really have an objection now, because this is an incomplete representation of General Petkovic's testimony. Bearing in mind the entire testimony, then you will be clear that this was the daily execution of policing matters, and that is clear. If she decides to give you a sentence after -- a sentence from different documents, you will get a distorted picture. I believe that my learned friend should respect the rules of additional questioning. She has to say what was said during the cross-examination. She should give us the page of the transcript, and that would enable us to follow. Now she is being allowed to engage in a new examination-in-chief, and I don't see a problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one word. The 4th Battalion -- the 4th Battalion of the Military Police that my learned friend has mentioned in her question, she's talking about a region, because that battalion was in Central Bosnia, and I never asked any questions about that during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an abuse of process. Normally, there should be sanctions from the Bench to the lawyers. Once the President has indicated that the lawyer can go on with the question, it is contempt of court, it is an abuse of process, and I suggest that such be entertained by the Trial Chamber. Otherwise, we are wasting a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to react. My learned friend Mr. Karnavas systematically poses as an arbiter in this courtroom, and he tries to teach us lessons about professionalism. I don't think it's fair, I don't think it's appropriate. And as far as the skills that Mr. Karnavas has or doesn't have, for four years now he has been showing us, in this courtroom, what he knows and what he doesn't know, and he has shown us that he's much better in theory than in practice. And I would like to remind Mr. Karnavas about his conduct when General Petkovic's cross -- re-examination started. I would like to ask the Trial Chamber, respectfully, to apply the same criteria to everybody in the courtroom, across the board. As far as my learned friend Mr. Karnavas is concerned, and his remarks, I do enjoy a status of the expert of the European Court for Human Rights, and I have also received an award of the American -- no, no. Your Honours, no. You have never, never reprimanded Mr. Karnavas when he spoke as he did, and you have been interrupted me so many times when I'm trying to defend my status and my rights in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you now why I have asked you to stop. On a personal note, I don't like lawyers criticising each other. It's not the arguments between the counsel I'm interested in, it's the fate of the people who are here. This is an extremely difficult and tall task for me. I am not going to try these people on the basis of what you've told each other, but on the merits of the case. And we are talking now about the military police. What I'm interested in are questions about the military police, that's it, full stop. That's why I asked you to stop. What I'm interested in is to know whether the military police was doing -- whether it was there, what it was doing. We know that there were several battalions. He is the commander of the 2nd Battalion. We know that there is a 4th Battalion. Maybe it works the same way; maybe it doesn't. We don't know. So please let your colleague put the question, and the Bench will then deliberate on the matter. We are interested in the fate of the people sitting here, the accused, not the skirmishes between Defence counsel. Ask your question now, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I hope that you still remember what I read out to you, sir. Tell me, please, where were you, in which operations zone?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I was in the North-West Herzegovina OZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Under whose command were you in that OZ?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were under the command of the OZ headquartered in Tomislavgrad, and our commander was Zeljko Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who did you receive orders from for your daily operations and duties?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our orders came from the commander of the operations zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: While you were in the North-West Herzegovina OZ as an active service battalion, were you engaged in combat in the North-West Herzegovina OZ?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, yes, we were also engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Under whose orders in the OZ North-West Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK [Resumed]
